Volunteers took the experiment at <https://github.com/chrplr/goxpyriment/tree/main/examples/Mental-Rotation-2D>


```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)  # makes the permutation tests reproducible
```

## Importing data into a single data frame

```{r}
files <- list.files("./data", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names=T)
print(length(files))
files
```

```{r}
read_all <- function(files) {
  bind_rows(lapply(files, function(f) {
    d <- read.csv(f)
    d$file_name <- f
    # the csv files store "true"/"false" in lowercase, which R does not parse as logical
    d$is_correct <- tolower(as.character(d$is_correct)) == "true"
    d
  })) %>%
    relocate(file_name)
}

data <- read_all(files)
head(data)
```

## Data inspection and cleaning

### Number of datapoints in each file

```{r}
data %>% count(file_name)
```

Let's remove the file with less than 40 datapoints

```{r}
files_ok <- setdiff(files, "Mental-Rotation-2D_sub-001_date-20260924-064330.csv")
```

```{r}
# we recreate the data frame with the new list of files
data <- read_all(files_ok)
head(data)
```

### Associating a unique subject_id to each file_name

```{r}
data <- data %>%
  mutate(subject_id = factor(match(file_name, unique(file_name))))
head(data)
```

## Error rates

Number of correct responses (out of 40) per subject:

```{r}
data %>%
  group_by(subject_id) %>%
  summarise(n_correct = mean(is_correct) * 40)
```

Let's inspect the errors

```{r}
data %>% filter(!is_correct)
```

## Reaction times

First, we inspect their distribution with an histogram

```{r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = rt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)
```

Then with a boxplot

```{r}
ggplot(data, aes(y = rt)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

### A look at the individual differences

```{r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = rt, y = 0, color = subject_id)) +
  # adds slight vertical spread so overlapping points remain visible
  geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.2, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

### Removing outliers

```{r}
data_clean <- data %>% filter(rt > 150, is_correct)
```

```{r}
print(nrow(data))                 # number of original data points
nrow(data) - nrow(data_clean)     # number of rejected data points
```

```{r}
medrt <- data_clean %>%
  group_by(subject_id) %>%
  summarise(rt = median(rt))
medrt
```

```{r}
ggplot(medrt, aes(x = rt, y = 0, color = subject_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

# Effects of angle and condition (same vs mirror)

```{r}
rts2 <- data_clean %>%
  group_by(subject_id, condition, angle) %>%
  summarise(rt = median(rt), .groups = "drop")
rts2
```

```{r}
rts3 <- data_clean %>%
  group_by(condition, angle) %>%
  summarise(rt = median(rt), .groups = "drop")
rts3
```

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
ggplot(rts3, aes(x = angle, y = rt, color = condition)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +  # adds points at each angle
  labs(x = "Angle", y = "Response Time (ms)",
       title = "Median RT by Angle across Conditions")
```

## Inferential analysis

**Are the differences statistically significant? That is, what is the probability that they are due to chance fluctuations?**

If we find that the probability is small, then we will reject the "null" hypothesis. The approach is called "Hypothesis testing".

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=12}
ggplot(rts2, aes(x = angle, y = rt, color = condition)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ subject_id, ncol = 3, labeller = label_both)  # one subplot per subject
```

Let's forget the distinction between mirror & same

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# individual results superposed (averaging over condition)
rts2 %>%
  group_by(subject_id, angle) %>%
  summarise(rt = mean(rt), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = angle, y = rt, color = subject_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# group result, with 95% confidence intervals (t-based)
mean_ci95 <- function(x) {
  ci <- t.test(x)$conf.int
  data.frame(y = mean(x), ymin = ci[1], ymax = ci[2])
}

ggplot(rts2, aes(x = angle, y = rt)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_ci95, geom = "ribbon", alpha = 0.2)
```

Let's compute p-values for the differences between angles conditions

```{r}
angles_rt <- rts2 %>%
  group_by(angle, subject_id) %>%
  summarise(rt = mean(rt), .groups = "drop")
angles_rt
```

```{r}
# rows are sorted by subject_id within each angle, so the vectors are paired
rt0   <- angles_rt %>% filter(angle == 0)   %>% pull(rt)
rt40  <- angles_rt %>% filter(angle == 40)  %>% pull(rt)
rt80  <- angles_rt %>% filter(angle == 80)  %>% pull(rt)
rt120 <- angles_rt %>% filter(angle == 120) %>% pull(rt)
rt160 <- angles_rt %>% filter(angle == 160) %>% pull(rt)
```

```{r}
rt40 - rt0
```

Let's compute the p-values using a permutation test (see <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_test>)

```{r}
my_permutation_test <- function(sample, npermutations = 10000) {
  # test if sample mean is significantly above 0 (one-tail test)
  obs_mean <- mean(sample)
  p <- length(sample)
  h0_dist <- replicate(npermutations,
                       mean(sample * sample(c(1, -1), size = p, replace = TRUE)))
  mean(h0_dist >= obs_mean)  # p-value
}
```

```{r}
print(mean(rt40 - rt0))
my_permutation_test(rt40 - rt0)
```

```{r}
my_permutation_test(rt80 - rt40)
```

```{r}
my_permutation_test(rt120 - rt80)
```

```{r}
my_permutation_test(rt160 - rt120)
```

## Using R's built-in tests

### Wilcoxon signed-rank test

The closest built-in equivalent of the sign-flipping permutation test is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which is a permutation test on the ranks of the differences (two-sided by default, like `scipy.stats.permutation_test`).

```{r}
wilcox.test(rt40 - rt0, mu = 0)
```

### Student t-test

See <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student%27s_t-test>

```{r}
# computing the t value "à la mano"
d <- rt40 - rt0
m <- mean(d)
s <- sd(d)      # R's sd() divides by n-1 (numpy's std() divides by n)
n <- length(d)
t <- m / s * sqrt(n)
print(c(m = m, s = s, n = n, t = t))

t.test(d, mu = 0)
```
